info.bio:
Jackie “Sonny” Wilson nació el 9 de Junio de 1934 en Detroit (Michigan, USA). La familia de Jackie, procedentes del Mississippi, es un poco peculiar; su padre, Jack, es un borrachuzo de mucho cuidado, además de no conocérsele actividad laboral; su “pobre” madre, Eliza Mae, perdió a sus dos anteriores hijos por lo que el pequeñín de Jackie era su vida entera.

Bien pequeño, el bueno de Jackie se ganaba la vida como buenamente podía y sabia, cantando.

scenes.name: Soul y R&B
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: El 1 de enero de 1966 el Top 3 estadounidense lo formaban «The Sound of Silence», «We Can Work It Out» y el «I Got You (I Feel Good)» de James Brown: discos futuristas los tres. A finales de mes Otis Redding se acercaba al Top 10 británico con su versión de «My Girl» de los Temptations.

scenes.name: Proto-funk
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: La revolución social inspiró la revolución rítmica: James Brown demostró que se podía usar una banda entera como una batería y llevar los polirritmos de vuelta a África, y los músicos que habían tocado para que otros bailaran se pusieron a bailar ellos. A mediados de los sesenta el nuevo groove se notó en «Respect» de Otis Redding, «Uptight» de Stevie Wonder o «Shotgun» de Junior Walker. «Funky Broadway» (1967) de Dyke and the Blazers, de Phoenix, fue el primer disco de baile negro que se llamó funky; Wilson Pickett lo pulió en Muscle Shoals y llegó al número 1 de R&B. Joe Tex pasó de las baladas al R&B caliente y al funk lascivo («Skinny Legs and All», «I Gotcha»). En Los Ángeles, Charles Wright y su Watts 103rd Street Rhythm Band dieron un funk suave y elegante («Express Yourself», sampleado por N.W.A.). Grupos instrumentales se volvían bandas: los Jazziacs neoyorquinos serían Kool & the Gang; los Ohio Untouchables, los Ohio Players; los Creators de Compton, War.

scenes.name: Antes del diluvio
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: La «edad oscura» del rock'n'roll: los rebeldes son sustituidos por ídolos adolescentes educados y el Brill Building devuelve el poder a los compositores profesionales. Pero en esos años se incuban la revolución futura: la guitarra fuzz de Link Wray, los bailes de moda (el twist), el rock instrumental de guitarras (Duane Eddy, Ventures, Shadows), el calipso y el primer ska, el doo-wop más inventivo (Coasters, Drifters, Five Royales), el nacimiento del soul (Sam Cooke, Ray Charles, Motown, Stax), el estudio como instrumento de Joe Meek y el surf de los Beach Boys y del «muro de sonido» de Phil Spector.

podcast.title: On-Stage Collapse in 1975
podcast.body: In 1975, while performing "Lonely Teardrops" and singing the line "my heart is crying," Wilson clutched his chest and collapsed on stage; initially mistaken for part of his act, he did not recover. "But then, in 1975, in the middle of performing lonely teardrops, right after singing the line, my heart is crying, he clutched his chest and collapsed."

podcast.body: Jackie Wilson was one of the deceased "forefathers" inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1987, alongside Aretha Franklin, who was notable for still being a current hitmaker at the time. "from deceased forefathers like Jackie Wilson"

podcast.title: Al Green's Management and Death
podcast.body: Local mobster Al Green took on Wilson's management, securing a contract with Bob Thiel at Decca Records by promising to also sign LaVern Baker, but Green died suddenly the day before Wilson's contract was meant to be signed. "Al Green died suddenly."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-Four: "Reet Petite" by Jackie Wilson

podcast.title: Appearance in "Go Johnny Go" Film
podcast.body: Jackie Wilson was one of the artists who appeared in the Alan Freed film "Go Johnny Go," alongside Richie Valens and other contemporary musical figures. "Valens appeared in the Alan Fried film Go Johnny Go, which featured Chuck Berry, Eddie Cochran, The Flamingos, and Jackie Wilson."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 73: "La Bamba" by Ritchie Valens

podcast.title: Attempt to Join The Four Ames (Four Tops)
podcast.body: After leaving Billy Ward and his Dominoes, Wilson attempted to join a vocal group with his cousin Levi Stubbs and distant relative Lawrence Payton, but his voice didn't blend well, sounding too similar to Stubbs. "Unfortunately, they found that Jackie's voice didn't blend well with the group."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-Four: "Reet Petite" by Jackie Wilson

podcast.title: Boxing-Inspired Dance Style
podcast.body: Wilson developed a unique, riveting dance style on stage, incorporating slides, sidesteps, and ducks learned from his boxing background, which allowed him to move from unexpected angles and dominate the stage. "He had a unique way of moving all his own, which he had learned in the boxing ring, where he'd learned to slide, sidestep, and duck away from other fighters, and to come at them from unexpected angles."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-Four: "Reet Petite" by Jackie Wilson

podcast.title: Career Dip and Revival
podcast.body: Wilson's career experienced a dip in the early 1960s with the British Invasion but saw a significant revival in 1967. "Although his career dipped in the early 60s with the British invasion. He then had a revival in 1967."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-Four: "Reet Petite" by Jackie Wilson

podcast.title: Coma and Vegetative State
podcast.body: Following his collapse, Wilson entered a coma from which he never fully recovered, remaining institutionalized in a persistent vegetative state for eight and a half years until his death. "For the next eight and a half years, Wilson was institutionalised."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-Four: "Reet Petite" by Jackie Wilson

podcast.title: Conspiracy Theories Around Collapse
podcast.body: Hypotheses for Wilson's collapse included induced hypertension from drinking salt water to sweat, but several people close to him believed he was poisoned by Nat Tarnapol, as Wilson was due to testify against Tarnapol in a grand jury ten days after the incident. "But several people close to Wilson believed that his collapse was somehow caused by Nat Turner-Paul, having him poisoned."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-Four: "Reet Petite" by Jackie Wilson

podcast.title: Danny Boy - Vocal Virtuosity
podcast.body: Wilson's favorite song to sing in talent contests was "Danny Boy," which remained in his set list throughout his life, used to showcase his vocal virtuosity by ornamenting the melody to an almost unrecognizable extent. "Wilson's favourite song to sing in talent contests was Danny Boy, which would remain in his set list until late in his life, and he would use that song as a way to show off his vocal virtuosity, ornamenting it to the point that the melody would become almost unrecognizable."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-Four: "Reet Petite" by Jackie Wilson

podcast.title: Dentures Flying Off On Stage
podcast.body: During a show where he was Dina Washington's support act, Wilson rolled his 'R' on the title of "Reet Petite" as he did on the record, causing his two front dentures to fly off, after which he never sang the song live again. "A one show where he was Dina Washington's support act, he rolled his R on the title of the song like he did on the record, and his two front dentures went flying off."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-Four: "Reet Petite" by Jackie Wilson

podcast.title: Discipline from Billy Ward
podcast.body: Billy Ward became a father figure to Wilson, teaching him breath control and instilling discipline for the first time in his life, which helped him mature as a performer. "Ward taught in breath control and became something of a father figure, giving him some discipline for the first time in his life."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-Four: "Reet Petite" by Jackie Wilson

podcast.title: Early Life as a Boxer
podcast.body: Wilson started out as a boxer in his teens before deciding to pursue singing instead, regularly performing at talent contests around Detroit. "Wilson started out as a boxer in his teens, but he quickly decided to move into singing instead."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-Four: "Reet Petite" by Jackie Wilson

podcast.title: Elvis Presley's Admiration
podcast.body: In 1956, Elvis Presley, during his own less successful first trip to Las Vegas, watched Wilson perform Elvis's hit "Don't Be Cruel" better than Elvis himself, leading Elvis to rave about Wilson on the famous Million Dollar Quartet tapes. "In the famous million dollar quartet tapes, you can hear Elvis raving about Wilson to Johnny Cash, Karl Perkins, and Jerry Lee Lewis."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-Four: "Reet Petite" by Jackie Wilson

podcast.title: Fallout with Tarnapol
podcast.body: Wilson's hit factory songwriters, Barry Gordy Jr., Billy Davis, and Gwen Gordy, fell out with manager Nat Tarnapol after discovering he was putting his own copyrighted songs on the B-sides of Wilson's records to collect royalties, refusing their demand to write both sides. "After they figured out that Tarnopol was putting songs to which he owned the copyright on the b-sides of all Wilson's records, so he could get royalties from the sales."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-Four: "Reet Petite" by Jackie Wilson

podcast.title: Inspiration for Music Icons
podcast.body: Jackie Wilson was a massively important performer who inspired Elvis Presley, Michael Jackson, and James Brown, providing a key link between 1950s R&B and 1960s Soul. "Someone who inspired Elvis, Michael Jackson, and James Brown, and who provides one of the key links between 50s R and B and 60s Soul."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-Four: "Reet Petite" by Jackie Wilson

podcast.title: James Brown's Bounced Check
podcast.body: James Brown initially sent a $1,000 check for Wilson's medical bills that bounced, but he paid the actual money after Wilson's common-law wife threatened to expose the incident to Jet Magazine. "James Brown sent a $1,000 check which bounced, but he cuffed up the actual money when Jackie's common-law wife said she was going to tell Jet Magazine about the bouncing check."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-Four: "Reet Petite" by Jackie Wilson

podcast.title: King Records Rejection and Later Recording
podcast.body: Talent scout Johnny Otis saw Wilson perform and tried to get him signed to King Records, but they initially only signed The Royals, recording a song Otis had written for Wilson with The Royals instead. He would later record with Billy Ward and his Dominoes for King Records. "King decided they only wanted to sign the royals, though they would sign Little Willie John a couple of years later."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-Four: "Reet Petite" by Jackie Wilson

podcast.title: Laryngitis During Recording "Reet Petite"
podcast.body: During the recording preparations for "Reet Petite," Wilson had laryngitis but insisted on singing the song a full octave higher than arranger Dick Jacobs suggested, despite initial skepticism from Jacobs and Bob Thiel. "Wilson couldn't demonstrate what he meant during the preparations for the session, as he had long in jatis, but he kept insisting that he should sing it a full octave higher than Jacobs initially suggested."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-Four: "Reet Petite" by Jackie Wilson

podcast.title: Las Vegas Residency Salary
podcast.body: While performing with The Dominoes in a two-year Las Vegas residency supporting Louis Prima and Keely Smith, the group earned $5,000 a week, but Wilson received a mere $90 a week as a salary. "Wilson was on a salary of only $90 a week."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-Four: "Reet Petite" by Jackie Wilson

podcast.title: Life-Saving Intervention
podcast.body: Cornel Gunter of The Coasters gave Jackie Wilson mouth-to-mouth resuscitation after his collapse, possibly saving his life, although some later questioned whether this was a good idea in retrospect. "Cornel Gunter of the coasters gave him mouth to mouth and possibly saved his life."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-Four: "Reet Petite" by Jackie Wilson

podcast.title: Mario Lanza's Influence
podcast.body: Wilson became obsessed with Italian American pop singer Mario Lanza, studying his performances and emulating his pseudo-operatic diction and projection, particularly after watching Lanza's 1951 film "The Great Caruso," while simultaneously acknowledging the commercial necessity of R&B as a black singer in Detroit. "Wilson studied Lanza's performances and he tried to emulate Lanza's diction and projection, but at the same time he was at heart an Arvind B performer and he also knew that as a black singer in Detroit in the early 50s, Arvind B was what he needed to do to make money."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-Four: "Reet Petite" by Jackie Wilson

podcast.title: Mother's Plea to Billy Ward
podcast.body: One story of Wilson joining Billy Ward and his Dominoes suggests his mother begged Ward to take him, fearing for his life due to his involvement in street trouble. "Ward used to tell, which is that one reason Wilson was picked for the group is that his mother begged Ward, saying that she was scared for the life of her son as he was getting into trouble on the streets."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-Four: "Reet Petite" by Jackie Wilson

podcast.title: Music Industry Support for Medical Bills
podcast.body: The music business rallied to help pay for Wilson's treatment, with reports of anonymous donations from Elvis Presley (unverified) and confirmed contributions from The Detroit Spinners ($5,000), Al Green (singer, $10,000), Stevie Wonder ($5,000), Gladys Knight ($2,500), Michael Jackson ($10,000), and Patti LaBelle ($1,200). "At first, the music business rallied round and helped pay for his treatment."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-Four: "Reet Petite" by Jackie Wilson

podcast.title: Nat Tarnapol's Deception Regarding Insurance
podcast.body: Nat Tarnapol and Brunswick Records provided no financial help for Wilson's medical bills and actively harmed his case by lying to Blue Cross Blue Shield, claiming Wilson had no earnings from them in the year prior to his collapse, thus preventing his medical bills from being covered by insurance. "They lied to Blue Cross Blue Shield, claiming that Wilson hadn't had any earnings from them in the year prior to his collapse, when he'd been in the studio and was owed regular union rates for recording sessions."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-Four: "Reet Petite" by Jackie Wilson

podcast.title: Nat Tarnapol's Rise to Power
podcast.body: After Al Green's death, office boy Nat Tarnapol audaciously took over Wilson's management, getting him signed to Brunswick (Decca's rock and roll subsidiary), and later used this leverage to become a co-owner of Brunswick. "More by Chutzpah the Nathan Else, Natt Tarnapoll, an office boy who had been employed by Green, managed to take over Wilson's management, just by saying that he was in charge now."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-Four: "Reet Petite" by Jackie Wilson

podcast.title: Stabbing Incident
podcast.body: Prior to joining Billy Ward and his Dominoes, Wilson had been stabbed in the chest by a sex worker, providing a reason for his mother's concerns for his safety. "Wilson had recently been stabbed in the chest by a sex worker."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-Four: "Reet Petite" by Jackie Wilson

podcast.title: Stage Name Change
podcast.body: Billy Ward changed Wilson's stage name from "Jack" or "Sonny" to "Jackie," as Ward felt "Sonny" "smacked of Uncle Tombery," a change Wilson initially disliked but later accepted, though he remained "Jack" or "Sonny" to close acquaintances. "Ward thought that being called Sunig smacked of Uncle Tombery, had decided that from this point on, Wilson's stage name was going to be Jackie."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-Four: "Reet Petite" by Jackie Wilson

podcast.title: Talent Contest Alliance
podcast.body: He was part of a loose association of musicians, including his cousin Levi Stubbs (later of The Royals), and Little Willie John, who would pre-arrange wins at talent shows. "They would all perform on the same talent shows and would agree among themselves who was going to win beforehand."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-Four: "Reet Petite" by Jackie Wilson

podcast.title: Unmarked Grave and Headstone
podcast.body: Wilson was initially buried in an unmarked grave after his death in 1984, but three years later, funds were raised for a headstone that reads, "No more lonely teardrops." "He was buried in an unmarked grave, but three years later, funds were raised for a headstone, which reads, no more lonely teardrops."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-Four: "Reet Petite" by Jackie Wilson

podcast.title: Vocal Influence on Eddie Holland
podcast.body: Eddie Holland's voice was noted for sounding similar to Jackie Wilson's. Barry Gordy initially used Holland as a demo singer for Wilson's songs and later tried to mold Holland into a "Wilson clone." "He was a singer who was known for having a similar sounding voice to that of Jackie Wilson"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
